extracted.intended_audience: elementary teachers, school librarians, and children's literature educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating, discussing, and selecting picture books for Caldecott consideration and classroom discussion, emphasizing how illustrations interact with text and the award's eligibility rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility: age, authorship/publication timing, and format
rubrics_metrics.description: A book for children age 0-14 written by an American author or published in the United States in the previous year. Since it’s an illustration award, the Caldecott Medal usually goes to a picture book but graphic novels and illustrated chapter books have won, too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More information, including a list of Award Criteria, is available on the ALA website. Eligibility focuses on audience (0-14), author/publisher national/publication timeframe, and illustrated format (picture books most common, but other illustrated forms may qualify).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary award criterion: quality of the illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The book with the best illustrations is awarded the Caldecott Medal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Caldecott is explicitly an illustration award. The committee may also name 1–4 Caldecott Honor books (tied for second place). A small committee of librarians reads hundreds of books and meets to select the winner; their deliberations are confidential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations should show, extend, or enhance the words
rubrics_metrics.description: How do the illustrations show, extend, or enhance the words of the story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested classroom procedure: read the story without sharing the pictures the first time, then read it a second time with the pictures to analyze how images interact with the text and augment meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial storytelling: illustrations can convey plot, characters, and meaning independently
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover up the words and 'read' the story using just the pictures. Were you able to understand the plot, characters, and meaning through the illustrations alone?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test gauges whether the visual narrative is sufficiently clear, expressive, and narratively complete to carry the story without text—an important aspect of illustration strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactions between words and pictures strengthen story elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the interactions between the words and the pictures in the book. How do the illustrations show, extend, or enhance the story, theme, plot, characters, setting, or mood?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate specific story elements (theme, plot, characters, setting, mood) and whether illustrations contribute uniquely or synergistically with the text to deepen reader understanding or emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of illustrative medium should relate to the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the verso (back side of the title page), end notes, or author’s website to learn more about how the illustrations were made. Does the choice of medium tie in to the story in some way?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how technique, materials, and production choices (e.g., collage, watercolor, digital) reflect or reinforce the book’s themes, tone, or narrative content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award process: committee selection and honor limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A small group of librarians from throughout the United States are chosen to serve on the Caldecott Award committee. They read hundreds of picture books before meeting in person to select the winner. No one knows exactly what happens in the discussions because committee members are sworn to secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that selection is by a deliberative committee process; practical implications for entrants/readers include that submissions are reviewed broadly by professional librarians and only a single medal and several honors are given each year.
